Reading A Lease Without Trusting The Clock

Anselmo Reis, 23 July 2025

A worker that holds a lease has to answer two questions that look like one: whether the lease is still mine, and whether it is still valid. Those are different questions, they fail differently, and a single comparison against the wall clock answers neither of them reliably.

The claim and the renewal both have to name the owner, so a worker that was paused long enough for its lease to expire cannot resurrect it afterwards:

UPDATE jobs
   SET lease_until = :now + :duration
 WHERE id = :id
   AND lease_owner = :owner
   AND lease_until > :now;

The third condition is the one people drop. Without it the statement renews a lease that has already been reclaimed by somebody else, and the two workers then both believe they hold it — which is exactly the state the lease existed to prevent.

Reclaiming on the other side

Reclaiming is the same statement read backwards. It takes the rows whose lease has run out, and it keeps the attempt count, because a crash loop that reset its own counter would run forever:

UPDATE jobs
   SET status      = 'queued',
       lease_until = NULL,
       lease_owner = NULL
 WHERE status      = 'running'
   AND lease_until <= :now;

In Go the renewal runs on a timer rather than on each loop iteration, so a handler that takes an hour keeps its lease without the loop having anything to do with it:

func (w *Worker) run(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
        renew := w.clock.NewTimer(renewInterval)
        defer renew.Stop()
        for {
                select {
                case err := <-done:
                        return err
                case <-renew.C():
                        if err := w.renew(ctx, job.ID); err != nil {
                                // Losing the lease is not a reason to stop: the
                                // handler is already running and the next claim
                                // will find the row, not this one.
                                w.log.Warn("renewing the lease", "err", err)
                        }
                        renew = w.clock.NewTimer(renewInterval)
                }
        }
}

The indentation in that last block is load bearing: the comment sits inside the error branch, and a reader who sees it one level out reads it as a comment about the whole loop. That is the whole argument for keeping code blocks intact.

What the clock is for

Every deadline above goes through an injected clock rather than through the system one, so a test walks the lease forward instead of sleeping through it. The wall clock then has exactly one job left, which is to be the thing the injected clock returns in production.
